panels.figure_caption: A 55-year-old man with no previous comorbidities presented with a 3-week history of cough, expectoration, fatigue, fever, night sweats, dyspnoea, and weight loss. A chest X-ray showed a miliary pattern. The patient was diagnosed with histoplasmosis after lung biopsy and positive serology.
in_text_mentions: miliary pattern; multiple small (<3 mm) pulmonary nodules of similar size that are randomly distributed throughout both lungs. Hematogenous spread of the fungus from re-infection from a very recent (usually <3 days) substantial exposure results in multiple foci of inflammation distributed throughout the lung, without lymphadenopathy or pleural effusion [35]. The differential diagnosis is wide, including tuberculosis, aspergillosis and coccidioidomycosis. Spontaneous resolution over several weeks or gradual deterioration and death may follow, hence antifungal treatment is usually given (Fig 4).

in_text_mentions: Micronodules with a random pattern of dissemination (miliary pattern) constitute a common presentation in various pulmonary mycoses, being described most frequently in histoplasmosis (Figure 6), paracoccidioidomycosis, coccidioidomycosis, and candidiasis, the last being more common in immunocompromised patients(4,20). The differential diagnoses of a miliary pattern include miliary metastases and the hematogenous dissemination of tuberculosis.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Panel A is CT angiography of same 31-year-old woman diagnosed with pulmonary histoplasmosis by two serologic methods, showing infiltrative mediastinal lesion with SVC compression and biopsy fibrosis, matching fibrosing mediastinitis described in-text as accumulation of fibrotic tissue in mediastinum. B: Panel B is PET/CT of same histoplasmosis patient showing mediastinal mass with high glycolytic activity, corresponding to fibrosing mediastinitis mass described in caption and in-text.
panels.attribution_text: Denning et al. Radiological features of chronic pulmonary histoplasmosis: Easily mistaken for tuberculosis.. PLoS neglected tropical diseases 2025. doi:10.1371/journal.pntd.0013219. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 6.
panels.figure_caption: A. A 31-year-old woman with no comorbidities presented with facial plethora and oedema of the cervical region and upper limbs. A CT angiography scan revealed a lesion measuring 5.4 × 3.0 × 4.4 cm, with approximately 75% reduction in the caliber of the superior vena cava. She was diagnosed with pulmonary histoplasmosis after positive serology results obtained by two different methods. The mediastinal biopsy revealed only fibrosis. B. PET/CT scan showed a mediastinal mass with high glycolytic activity.
in_text_mentions: Fibrosing mediastinitis is a serious presentation associated with pulmonary histoplasmosis [16,18,35,87]. It is visualized as the accumulation of fibrotic tissue in the mediastinum structures, especially the middle mediastinum (Fig 6). This can lead to compression of various mediastinal structures such as the superior vena cava [31]. Fibrosing mediastinitis caused by H. capsulatum is the most common benign cause of superior vena cava syndrome [35]. The chest X-ray usually shows mediastinal widening [18,35,88].

panels.rationale: H&E-stained histology of intestinal mucosa shows intracellular small budding yeasts of H. capsulatum within macrophages/histiocytes, classic for disseminated histoplasmosis; article title identifies the case as disseminated histoplasmosis misdiagnosed as visceral leishmaniasis. [raw subtype: disseminated]
panels.attribution_text: Calvopiña et al. A Fatal Case of Disseminated Histoplasmosis by Histoplasma capsulatum var. capsulatum Misdiagnosed as Visceral Leishmaniasis-Molecular Diagnosis and Identification.. Pathogens (Basel, Switzerland) 2023. doi:10.3390/pathogens12091112. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: The present image from a histological section of the intestinal mucosa wrongly reported the presence of Leishmania amastigotes. The characteristic kinetoplasts of Leishmania, which typically exhibit stronger staining than the nucleus, are not observed in these oval structures. Under hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining at 100× magnification, the ovoid yeasts of H. capsulatum are visible. Yeasts measure 2 to 4 μm, have unstained cell walls with a distinct refractile capsule, and exhibit narrow-based budding. They are predominantly found phagocytosed within macrophages and histiocytes, often forming clusters of numerous organisms. Occasionally, they may also be observed in extracellular spaces [28].

panels.rationale: Grocott-stained histopathology from a patient with progressive disseminated histoplasmosis shows a necrotizing bronchial mucosal granuloma containing numerous fungal structures consistent with H. capsulatum; the panel is a real patient image and qualifies for the histoplasmosis library.
panels.attribution_text: Castro et al. Histoplasmosis: No Longer Just a Disease of the Immunocompromised.. Cureus 2025. doi:10.7759/cureus.78260. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 5.
panels.figure_caption: Necrotizing granuloma of the bronchial mucosa, featuring numerous fungal structures stained purple in multiple areas, with one highlighted by the blue arrow. Grocott staining, 20x magnification.
in_text_mentions: Pathology results revealed that both lesions were associated with a fungal infection, with morphological and histochemical characteristics consistent with H. capsulatum (Figure 5, Figure 6). A review of older medical records uncovered a previous bone marrow biopsy that had revealed necrotizing granulomas. Based on these findings, a diagnosis of progressive disseminated histoplasmosis was made, considering the involvement of the lungs, pharynx, larynx, bone marrow, and associated hepatosplenomegaly.

panels.rationale: Silver-stained bone marrow smear from a patient with confirmed disseminated histoplasmosis (positive urine histoplasma antigen, negative leishmania/cryptococcal/HIV workup) showing budding yeast forms within and released from mononuclear cells. The caption and in-text evidence directly attribute the fungal morphology to histoplasmosis, matching the classic intracellular budding yeasts finding. Single real patient histology image, no third-party copyright.

panels.figure_caption: Budding fungus from intracellular to extracellular space on silver staining of mononuclear cells on bone marrow smear (100x magnification).
in_text_mentions: hly suspicious for a fungal infection (Figure 2). Encapsulated organisms with narrow based budding positive on silver stain were confirmed which clinched the diagnosis of disseminated histoplasmosis (Figure 3). Urine histoplasma antigen was sent which was >25 U/mL. Giemsa staining, immunohistochemistry, and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for leishmania were all negative. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: H&E-stained adrenal biopsy section showing small intracellular Histoplasma yeast forms with lucent halos clustered in macrophages; the textbook histologic presentation of adrenal histoplasmosis in this immunocompetent patient. B: Higher-magnification H&E adrenal biopsy section confirming intracellular Histoplasma yeast forms within macrophages; classic histology of adrenal histoplasmosis. C: PAS-stained adrenal biopsy section from a necrotic area showing spilled, haphazardly arranged Histoplasma yeast forms; consistent with necrotizing adrenal histoplasmosis. D: GMS-stained adrenal biopsy section from necrotic tissue demonstrating Histoplasma yeasts with narrow-based budding, a pathognomonic feature confirming adrenal histoplasmosis.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (a, b, c). a: Human skin biopsy H&E showing pandermal granulomatous inflammation with epithelioid histiocytes and Langerhans giant cells; the article confirms Histoplasma by PAS/GMS morphology and culture, supporting histoplasmosis. b: PAS-stained human tissue shows intracellular oval narrow-neck budding yeast forms, the textbook histologic signature of Histoplasma; in-text and culture confirmation support histoplasmosis. c: GMS stain from the confirmed skin biopsy shows a narrow-neck budding fungal organism, supporting histoplasmosis with explicit Histoplasma attribution in the in-text description.

in_text_mentions: (eight weeks later) showed a CD4 count of 124 cells/µL with a viral load of less than 20 copies/mL. Urinalysis and urine histoplasma antigen test were negative. Histology of the liver, larynx and sections of the skin demonstrated pandermal necrotising granulomatous inflammation. Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver and PAS stains revealed a relative paucity of intracellular oval, narrow-neck budding fungal organisms morphologically in keeping with Histoplasma capsulatum var. capsulatum (Figure 2a and b). Fungal culture of liver, epiglottis ulcer and skin confirmed the diagnosis of histoplasmosis.

in_text_mentions: psied for histopathologic evaluation. Hematoxylin-and-eosin (H&E) stain demonstrated necrotizing granulomas with ulceration and lymphocytic infiltrate (Figure 3) and multinucleate giant cells (Figure 4). Grocott’s methenamine silver stain demonstrated no evidence of fungal elements. No additional stains were performed. Indirect immunofluorescence was negative for antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA). The ACE level was negative. Sedimentation rate, CRP, vitamin D, vitamin B12, folate, and ferritin were within normal limits. PCR was negative for HSV, VZV, CMV, and coxsackievirus A and B.

in_text_mentions: inflammatory infiltrate composed of lymphocytes and histiocytes, some epithelioid cells, in a compact nodular arrangement, interspersed with some thick collagen fibers and small blood capillaries occupying the superficial and mid-dermis. Granulomas containing Langhans-type giant cells were also observed. H&E staining revealed in the superficial and middle dermis, a granulomatous-type infiltrate, as well as the presence of small yeasts (Figure 2). Grocott's stain highlighted the presence of small spores surrounded by a transparent halo, isolated and clustered inside the histiocytes (Figure 3).

in_text_mentions: Clinical examination showed a prostrated and immunosuppressed patient with feeding difficulty. Oral examination revealed ulcerated lesions, caries and purulent exudate on the dorsal surface of tongue and on the hard palate. In addition, an erosive whitish lesion, typical of opportunistic lesions, was observed on the skin of the left forearm. A tongue biopsy was carried out for histopathological analysis in addition to the routine laboratory exams that were prescribed. The rapid HIV test and the specific test (Western blot) were positive, confirming a diagnosis of AIDS (Figures 1A, 1B and 1C).

The routine histopathological analysis showed the presence of clear haloes and hyphae, which, in combination with the clinical characteristics, confirmed a diagnosis of histoplasmosis (Figure 1D). Drug treatment was initiated with three daily mouth washes of nystatin (500,000IU), and the patient was referred to the medical clinic for AIDS treatment. A month later, the family reported that the patient had died.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Axial FDG PET-CT shows FDG-avid hilar and subcarinal lymph nodes in a patient with progressive disseminated histoplasmosis; the controlled vocabulary lacks a specific key for this nodal avidity pattern. B: Coronal FDG PET-CT demonstrates enlarged FDG-avid bilateral adrenal glands and hepatosplenomegaly, compatible with disseminated histoplasmosis. C: CECT shows centrilobular nodules in the right lower lobe in the setting of progressive disseminated histoplasmosis; the controlled vocabulary lacks an exact centrilobular nodule key. D: CECT demonstrates bilateral adrenal enlargement with internal necrosis, a classic manifestation of disseminated histoplasmosis.

panels.rationale: Single histologic image from a case of disseminated histoplasmosis involving the brain. Caption and in-text report caseating granuloma with histoplasma in brain tissue, matching the histoplasmosis caseating epithelioid granuloma finding. The green arrow is an annotation, not a separate panel. No age, ethnicity, or skin tone information is provided in the caption or in-text mentions.

in_text_mentions: he patient was started on intravenous amphotericin for treating disseminated histoplasmosis. Blood cultures were negative for fungal growth. His condition worsened, and he continued to have altered sensorium, rectal bleeding, and developed respiratory distress needing mechanical ventilation. A cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) study was negative for organisms. The patient underwent left temporal craniotomy and resection of the temporal mass, and the tissue biopsy revealed caseating granuloma with histoplasmosis on the PAS stain (Figure 5) and the presence of histoplasmosis on the GMS stain (Figure 6).

panels.rationale: Single-panel PAS-stained intestinal biopsy histology from a real patient with confirmed gastrointestinal histoplasmosis. The image visibly shows histiocytes packed with small intracellular PAS-positive yeast forms (white arrows), the classic microscopic presentation of Histoplasma capsulatum. Disease attribution is directly supported by the caption and in-text confirmation of Histoplasma capsulatum in the resected jejunum. [raw subtype: gastrointestinal]

in_text_mentions: tment resulted in marked improvement of the cutaneous lesions, with no infusion-related reactions or significant drug-related adverse effects documented. One week later, the patient developed gastrointestinal bleeding and an acute abdomen, necessitating an exploratory laparotomy. Intraoperative findings revealed a jejunal perforation, and segmental resection of the affected small bowel was performed. Histopathological examination demonstrated acute-on-chronic enteritis with transmural perforation associated with Histoplasma capsulatum, confirming gastrointestinal histoplasmosis (Figures 4, 5).

panels.rationale: Giemsa-stained histologic section of a biopsied mediastinal lymph node showing small intracellular yeast forms within histiocytes, explicitly attributed to Histoplasma capsulatum in the in-text mention. This is the classic histopathologic presentation of disseminated histoplasmosis in a kidney transplant patient. White block arrows annotate the yeast forms.
panels.attribution_text: Trimarchi et al. Belatacept and mediastinal histoplasmosis in a kidney transplant patient.. Journal of nephropathology 2016. doi:10.15171/jnp.2016.15. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
in_text_mentions: was performed and a node biopsied for histological and microbiological assessment. After 24 hours small intracellular yeast compatible with Histoplasma capsulatum were reported in Giemsa stain in tissue samples (Figure 1). Fungal colonies were observed after 10 days of incubation of the mediastinal node. At 35°C, creamy yeast colonies were observed, while at 28°C the colonies developed aerial white cottony mycelium (Figure 2). The patient was started on intravenous amphotericin B therapy and later switched to oral fluconazol. Belatacept was not discontinued and kidney function remains normal.

panels.rationale: Single frontal chest radiograph from a real patient in a case report titled 'Disseminated Histoplasmosis: The Great Mimicker in Patients With Advanced HIV Disease.' The caption and in-text explicitly attribute the bilateral diffuse micronodular (miliary) interstitial opacities, marked by black arrows, to pulmonary involvement in disseminated histoplasmosis, matching the vocabulary finding for miliary pulmonary micronodules. No third-party indicator, no competing disease attribution, and the image is diagnostic quality. [raw subtype: disseminated]

in_text_mentions: Abdominal examination revealed hepatosplenomegaly. Subsequently, the patient developed mixed dysphagia and a fever of 38.3°C, which prompted hospital admission. Laboratory workup upon admission revealed pancytopenia, with leukopenia (white blood cell count 2.70 ×10³/µL; reference range: 4-10 ×10³/µL), normocytic normochromic anemia (hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL; reference range: 11-16 g/dL), and thrombocytopenia (platelet count 106 ×10³/µL; reference range: 130-400 ×10³/µL). A chest X-ray (Figure 2) documented a diffuse micronodular interstitial pattern.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (a, b, c, d). a: Human bone marrow H&E from a patient with culture-proven Histoplasma capsulatum infection (article title and in-text: blood cultures positive for Histoplasma capsulatum); panel shows increased histiocytes in loose aggregates without formed granulomas, consistent with the unorganized histiocytic infiltrate of disseminated histoplasmosis. b: CD163 immunohistochemistry on the same patient's bone marrow biopsy highlighting the increased histiocyte population; disease attribution is explicit from the caption, in-text mention, and culture-proven Histoplasma capsulatum infection in this histoplasmosis case report. c: GMS-stained bone marrow section from the same patient showing numerous budding yeast forms with morphology explicitly stated as consistent with Histoplasma; this is the textbook histologic presentation of histoplasmosis and is directly captioned. d: Second GMS-stained bone marrow field from the same patient showing budding yeast...
panels.attribution_text: Untanu et al. Histoplasmosis-Induced Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis in an Adult Patient: A Case Report and Review of the Literature.. Case reports in infectious diseases 2016. doi:10.1155/2016/1358742. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: (a) Bone marrow biopsy with increased number of histiocytes, focally present in loose aggregates, hematoxylin and eosin stain, 40x. (b) CD163 staining on bone marrow biopsy highlighting histiocytes. (c)-(d) GMS (Gomori-Methenamine Silver) staining on bone marrow biopsy. Numerous budding fungal organisms with morphology consistent with Histoplasma are present.
in_text_mentions: ratio, megakaryocytes were slightly increased in number, and increased proportion of histiocytes, focally also forming loose aggregates, were noted. Histiocytes had foamy cytoplasm and in a few cells intracytoplasmic cellular debris was also identified. Well defined granulomas or areas of necrosis were not seen (Figures 2(a) and 2(b)). Staining for fungal organisms (GMS) revealed budding yeast with morphology consistent with Histoplasma. Further CD163 immunostain highlighted increased proportion of histiocytes in the bone marrow biopsy. Blood cultures were positive for Histoplasma capsulatum.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: H&E 400X of a human omental biopsy showing small intracellular Histoplasma yeasts (arrows); in-text confirms yeasts characteristic of Histoplasma spp. Real patient histopathology of the target disease. B: H&E 400X of the same omental biopsy showing Histoplasma yeasts within necrosis areas, consistent with the in-text description of necrotizing caseous granulomas. Real patient histopathology of the target disease. C: H&E 400X showing macrophages containing yeasts, i.e., yeast-packed histiocytes with intracellular Histoplasma forms in the omental biopsy. Real patient histopathology of the target disease. D: Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver stain at 400X showing black round-to-oval yeasts (4–6 μm) characteristic of Histoplasma spp., confirming the diagnosis in this human omental biopsy.

panels.figure_caption: Detection of Histoplasma spp. infection in biopsy. A. The staining reveals the yeast as small diffuse purple dots indicated by the arrows due to cell overlay, hematoxilin and eosine, 400X. B. They are also observed in necrosis areas, hematoxilin and eosine, 400X. C. Presence of macrophages containing yeasts, hematoxilin and eosine, 400X. D. in_text_mentions: ndings also included septic shock, generalized peritonitis, and turbid peritoneal fluid consistent with ascites and suggestive of peritoneal carcinomatosis originating from the transverse colon. Peritoneal fluid was collected for culture; the media used included blood culture bottles and direct plating on Sabouraud dextrose agar, incubated for three weeks, the result was negative. A segmental jejunal resection with jejunostomy was performed, and an omental biopsy was obtained for histopathological examination (figures 2 and 3). Both blood and peritoneal fluid cultures yielded negative results.

Microscopic analysis of the omental biopsy with hematoxylin and eosin staining revealed necrotizing caseous granulomas suggestive of yeast presence, confirmed by specific Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver staining, showing black oval yeasts characteristic of Histoplasma spp. (figure 3). The result of this test took two weeks; unfortunately, by the time it was available, the patient had already died.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: H&E (100X) of an omental biopsy from a patient diagnosed with gastrointestinal histoplasmosis; the in-text explicitly attributes figure 2 to 'necrotizing caseous granulomas.' Granulomatous inflammation is a recognized histopathologic manifestation of histoplasmosis and maps to the vocabulary finding caseating epithelioid granuloma. Confidence is tempered by the in-text caveat that such granulomas are histologically indistinguishable from peritoneal tuberculosis, but the case diagnosis and disease-focused article title support attribution to histoplasmosis. B: H&E (100X) showing caseous necrosis with granular debris, the central necrotic component of a caseating granuloma. Tied by the in-text to the omental biopsy (figure 2) of a gastrointestinal histoplasmosis patient. Caseating epithelioid granuloma is a recognized histoplasmosis manifestation present in the vocabulary. Same tuberculosis-indistinguishability caveat applies, but the case...

in_text_mentions: ndings also included septic shock, generalized peritonitis, and turbid peritoneal fluid consistent with ascites and suggestive of peritoneal carcinomatosis originating from the transverse colon. Peritoneal fluid was collected for culture; the media used included blood culture bottles and direct plating on Sabouraud dextrose agar, incubated for three weeks, the result was negative. A segmental jejunal resection with jejunostomy was performed, and an omental biopsy was obtained for histopathological examination (figures 2 and 3). Both blood and peritoneal fluid cultures yielded negative results.

The omental biopsy revealed the presence of necrotizing caseous granulomas (figure 2). The frequency of granulomas was reported in 39.3% of HIV-positive patients reviewed in the literature by Assi et al. (2006) and in 44.4% of the patients evaluated in their study. However, patients with advanced cellular immunodeficiency may not present the typical characteristics of granulomatous inflammation and may not be observable 4. These granulomas are also common in peritoneal tuberculosis, but histologically, distinguishing them from gastrointestinal histoplasmosis is not possible 2.

panels.rationale: H&E-stained bone marrow aspirate from a real patient showing a histiocyte packed with small intracellular yeasts exhibiting clear halo-like unstained zones around amaranth nuclei, explicitly described as highly suggestive of Histoplasma capsulatum. This is a textbook presentation of intracellular budding yeasts in histiocytes in disseminated histoplasmosis. [raw subtype: disseminated]
panels.attribution_text: Yang et al. Colonic involvement in disseminated histoplasmosis of an immunocompetent adult: case report and literature review.. BMC infectious diseases 2013. doi:10.1186/1471-2334-13-143. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Hematoxylin and eosin stained bone marrow aspirate.
in_text_mentions: Hematoxylin and eosin stained bone marrow aspirate demonstrated oval or round organisms with amaranth nuclei and capsule-like unstained halos around them, confined to the cytoplasm of phagocytes, which is highly suggestive of Histoplasmosis capsulatum (Figure 1). Sections of bone marrow biopsy stained with PAS (periodic acid-schiff) and GMS (Gomori methenamine silver) were both positive, which was compatible with a diagnosis of histoplasmosis.

panels.rationale: Real patient histopathology from the article's reported case of disseminated histoplasmosis with colonic involvement. GMS-stained colon biopsy at ×40 shows numerous small silver-positive intracellular yeast-like structures within increased numbers of histiocytes, the classic histologic hallmark of Histoplasma capsulatum infection. Disease attribution is directly supported by the caption, the in-text description (GMS/PAS positive, Giemsa negative), and the article title. Adult age group taken from the article title ('immunocompetent adult'). No skin, ethnicity, or annotation elements are present.
panels.attribution_text: Yang et al. Colonic involvement in disseminated histoplasmosis of an immunocompetent adult: case report and literature review.. BMC infectious diseases 2013. doi:10.1186/1471-2334-13-143. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) stained colon biopsy specimen (magnification × 40).
in_text_mentions: Gastrointestinal endoscopy was subsequently performed, and colonoscopy showed strictures, edematous mucosa and diffuse aphthoid ulcers measuring 0.5-1.0 cm in diameter scattered throughout the mucous membrane of the colon (Figure 2). Biopsy specimens of the colon identified numerous yeast-like structures within increased numbers of histiocytes staining positive for PAS stain, and GMS stain but Giemsa stain negative (Figure 3), indicating granulomatous inflammation induced by mycotic infection, which was consistent with histoplasmosis.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: H&E microphotograph (20×) of a human adrenal biopsy showing foamy histiocytes packed with small round-to-oval fungal elements with a halo (arrows), the classic histologic picture of Histoplasma infection; article title and in-text confirm adrenal histoplasmosis with PET-guided biopsy. [raw subtype: adrenal] b: PAS-stained microphotograph (20×) of the same human adrenal biopsy highlighting intracellular Histoplasma yeast forms within foamy histiocytes (arrows); PAS positivity and halo morphology confirm histoplasmosis in adrenal tissue. [raw subtype: adrenal]

panels.figure_caption: Microphotograph of the biopsy specimen in (a) haematoxylin and eosin (20×) staining and (b) periodic acid–Schiff (20×) staining showing infiltration of foamy histiocytes containing spores of histoplasma (arrows).
in_text_mentions: es. A posterior paravertebral percutaneous route was chosen owing to the proximity of the lesion, ease of approach as well as the consideration of safe trajectory. Three fragments of adrenal tissue were obtained and the histopathology of two fragments showed focal polymorph-rich inflammatory infiltrate admixed with scattered foamy histiocytes and occasional giant cells. These foamy histiocytes showed increased small round to oval fungal elements with a halo corresponding to the morphology of histoplasma, which was highlighted by periodic acid–Schiff stain (Figure 3). One fragment was necrotic.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Left adrenal biopsy H&E from a human patient with disseminated histoplasmosis; caption and in-text explicitly attribute the small round shadowlike microorganisms (yellow arrows) to Histoplasma, consistent with HP. Real patient histopathology, clear disease attribution and classic intracellular yeast morphology. B: Same left adrenal biopsy as panel A, GMS silver stain highlighting Histoplasma yeasts black (red arrows); caption and in-text confirm organisms turned dark black with GMS, consistent with HP. Real patient histopathology with explicit histoplasmosis attribution; dense black staining visually supports a diffuse yeast-packed histiocytic infiltrate.

in_text_mentions: Subsequently, a left adrenal biopsy was performed and stained with hematoxylin and eosin, demonstrating small, round, shadowlike microorganisms that turned dark black when stained with GMS—consistent with HP (Figure 5). Serological tests revealed positive histoplasma antibody, with yeast phase antibody titer of 1:8, positive urine histoplasma antigen, and positive adrenal gland histoplasma antigen. At this point, the diagnosis of disseminated HP was made.

He subsequently began treatment with ibrutinib in March 2016, which he continued until February 2020.

in_text_mentions: thus started on conventional intravenous Amphotericin-B at a dose of 1 mg/kg/day. However, on the same day, he succumbed to his illness. Postmortem biopsies of lung, liver, and spleen were taken (with consent of the relatives) all of which showed numerous intracellular spherical organisms in the histiocytes present in the lung interstitium, sinusoidal Kupffer cells of liver, and splenic macrophages, morphologically compatible with Histoplasma (Figure 3). The final diagnosis of chronic progressive disseminated histoplasmosis, involving liver, spleen, lung, GIT, bone marrow, and skin, was made.

panels.rationale: High-power periodic acid-Schiff stain of the patient's abdominal skin biopsy shows a perivascular infiltrate of histiocytes with scattered small intracellular yeast forms, the classic histopathologic signature of histoplasmosis. In-text mention links this biopsy to the patient's progressive disseminated histoplasmosis (yeast forms within monocytes on peripheral smear; article title names disseminated histoplasmosis). Real single-panel patient histopathology image with black and red arrow annotations; disease attribution and findings are directly caption-supported, and prior caption triage routes it to keep. [raw subtype: disseminated]

panels.rationale: Single axial chest CT from a real patient with a red arrow marking the right lung. Caption and article title explicitly attribute the diffuse micronodular pulmonary changes to disseminated histoplasmosis, and the in-text description confirms micronodularity (with cavitary nodules, bronchiectasis and ground-glass change) predominantly in the right lung. The miliary/diffuse micronodular pattern is a classic radiologic presentation of disseminated histoplasmosis, so the panel is included with high confidence. [raw subtype: disseminated]

In the following days, from both the peripheral vein blood and bone marrow aspirate, cultures on Sabouraud dextrose agar incubated at 30°C and grew H. capsulatum (Figure 3).

panels.rationale: Single-panel clinical photograph of a patient's face (eyes redacted with a black bar for anonymization, not a diagnostic annotation) showing multiple discrete hyperpigmented papulonodular lesions with umbilication, central necrosis, and crusting on the cheeks, nose, perioral skin, and chin. The disease-focused article title ('Disseminated histoplasmosis with conjunctival involvement...') together with the panel-specific caption and in-text description establishes that these facial lesions are a cutaneous manifestation of disseminated histoplasmosis. The umbilicated, necrotic-centered (molluscum-like) papule is a recognized classic presentation of cutaneous histoplasmosis in disseminated disease. No age or ethnicity is stated in the caption or in-text; visible facial skin is adequately lit and appears medium brown. [raw subtype: disseminated]

in_text_mentions: upon palpation in the right upper quadrant but not in any other quadrant. Later, edema in both of his pelvic limbs along with jaundice on the skin and mucous membranes (ophthalmic and oral) was added to the symptoms. The patient was admitted to the general surgery department with suspected cholecystitis. Subsequent thoracic and abdominal tomography revealed bilateral pulmonary infiltrates alongside hepatomegaly (25 cm in length) and splenomegaly (15 cm in length). The tomography report detailed areas of consolidation, ground glass opacities, and multiple nodular images in the lungs (Figure 1).

A simple computerized axial tomography is presented, in a high-resolution window, in a five-vessel section. At the lung level, lesions compatible with a nodular pattern can be seen, with improvement compared to a previous study shown in Figure 1.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (a, b, c, d). a: Grocott-stained naso-maxillar biopsy from the reported patient; the figure is the microbiologic confirmation of Histoplasma capsulatum (culture/PCR) in disseminated histoplasmosis, so the fungal-yeast finding is attributable to histoplasmosis. Lower-power Grocott view of the infected tissue. b: Gram Wegert-stained section of the same naso-maxillar biopsy; the in-text statement that microscopic examination of Fig. 3 revealed fungal yeasts, together with culture/PCR confirmation of H. capsulatum, attributes the finding to histoplasmosis. c: High-power Grocott stain clearly shows small intracellular budding yeasts within histiocytes, the textbook diagnostic appearance of Histoplasma capsulatum; disease attribution is confirmed by mycological culture and PCR in the article. d: PAS-stained section of the same naso-maxillar biopsy; PAS demonstrates fungal organisms and the figure is the yeast-revealing microscopy confirmed as H. capsulatum...

panels.rationale: Single-panel chest radiograph of a real patient showing an extensive bilateral nodular pattern. The prior caption triage identifies this as a manifestation of disseminated histoplasmosis, and the diffuse micronodular/miliary pulmonary pattern matches the vocabulary finding histoplasmosis_miliary_pulmonary_micronodules. The article title leads with disseminated histoplasmosis. Confidence is moderated because the article also reports concurrent pulmonary tuberculosis and CMV disease, so the radiographic nodular pattern is not exclusively attributed to histoplasmosis in the caption; however, miliary pulmonary micronodules are a recognized classic presentation of disseminated histoplasmosis and the prior triage route is keep.

panels.rationale: Single axial CT angiogram of the chest from a real human patient (article primary disease histoplasmosis). The image visibly shows bilateral multifocal/diffuse nodular pulmonary infiltrates with a prominent, measured (22 mm) right hilar lymph node, findings consistent with pulmonary histoplasmosis; the caption does not attribute the panel to another disease and the prior triage kept it. Disease attribution is tempered because the article describes Cryptococcus/Histoplasmosis co-infection, so the infiltrates are not organism-specific; confidence is moderate. The diffuse nodular infiltrate pattern is mapped to the closest vocabulary entry (miliary/diffuse nodular pulmonary micronodules), and the hilar lymphadenopathy is captured as a proposed finding since no non-calcified hilar-node vocabulary term exists.

panels.rationale: Real portable AP semi-erect chest radiograph of the article's patient with a disease-focused title of disseminated histoplasmosis. The yellow-arrow right upper lobe irregular calcification is a healed/calcified pulmonary granuloma, a specific histoplasmosis manifestation present in the vocabulary ('Pulmonary focus of calcification' synonym), so it is attributed to histoplasmosis. The red-arrow left basilar atelectasis and blue-arrow left hemidiaphragm elevation are nonspecific acute/critical-illness findings not in the vocabulary and are placed in proposed_findings rather than driving attribution. Calcified granulomas are not disease-exclusive, so confidence is moderate. No skin, ethnicity, or explicit age is assessable/stated.

The caption documents bilateral adrenal masses (4 cm each), hepatomegaly (red arrow), splenomegaly (blue arrow) and enlarged pericaval lymph nodes. Bilateral adrenal enlargement is a specific, recognized CT manifestation of disseminated histoplasmosis and matches the provided vocabulary finding; hepatosplenomegaly and pericaval lymphadenopathy are clearly present but absent from the vocabulary, so they are listed as proposed findings. No third-party copyright, animal model, control, diagram or other-disease panel is involved. [raw subtype: disseminated]

Cutaneous nodules are a recognized manifestation of disseminated disease and the panel is presented within a histoplasmosis case figure; the prior triage also attributes all panels to the same disease. in_text_mentions: A 49-year-old lady presented with generalized myalgias and arthritis of two-year duration, which had responded partly to glucocorticoids. She reported to us in December 2018, two years into the illness; with worsening myalgia and ulcerative eyelid lesions following a glucocorticoid taper. Eventually, it turned out that anti-synthetase syndrome was the primary diagnosis with Histoplasma infections in the muscles and eye (Figure 1). We herewith present the course of her illness and a review of Histoplasmosis of the muscle in literature.

d numerous budding yeast cells suggestive of Histoplasma Capsulatum. The skin biopsy from the lower eyelid ulcer yielded granulomatous inflammation. Giemsa stain again showed numerous budding yeast cells suggestive of Histoplasmosis (Figure 1). Ultrasound of both thighs and arms at the sites of tenderness suggested multiple hypoechoic lesions with loss of standard fibrillar architecture of muscles (Figure 1). Thus, the patient had pyomyositis, and sonographic drainage confirmed the presence of pus. A Giemsa stained smear showed numerous budding yeast cells suggestive of Histoplasma capsulatum.

in_text_mentions: The patient was empirically started on antibiotics and octreotide infusion for cirrhotic variceal bleeding. He continued to have rectal bleeding, and in the following day, he underwent a colonoscopy that showed significant ulceration (multiple ulcers 5mm-1cm) in the rectum, sigmoid colon, and descending colon; hemostatic clips were placed. Ulcers were biopsied. Rectal biopsy reported active colitis and was positive for histoplasmosis on Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS; Figure 1) and Grocott's methenamine silver (GMS) stain (Figure 2).

in_text_mentions: he patient was started on intravenous amphotericin for treating disseminated histoplasmosis. Blood cultures were negative for fungal growth. His condition worsened, and he continued to have altered sensorium, rectal bleeding, and developed respiratory distress needing mechanical ventilation. A cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) study was negative for organisms. The patient underwent left temporal craniotomy and resection of the temporal mass, and the tissue biopsy revealed caseating granuloma with histoplasmosis on the PAS stain (Figure 5) and the presence of histoplasmosis on the GMS stain (Figure 6).

panels.rationale: Single-panel Grocott-stained intestinal biopsy histology from a real patient. The caption explicitly identifies small oval yeast-like structures compatible with Histoplasma spp. (white arrows), and the in-text confirms acute-on-chronic enteritis with transmural perforation associated with Histoplasma capsulatum, establishing gastrointestinal histoplasmosis in the setting of disseminated disease. The image clearly shows classic intracellular budding yeasts and a diffuse yeast-packed histiocytic infiltrate. [raw subtype: gastrointestinal]

in_text_mentions: tment resulted in marked improvement of the cutaneous lesions, with no infusion-related reactions or significant drug-related adverse effects documented. One week later, the patient developed gastrointestinal bleeding and an acute abdomen, necessitating an exploratory laparotomy. Intraoperative findings revealed a jejunal perforation, and segmental resection of the affected small bowel was performed. Histopathological examination demonstrated acute-on-chronic enteritis with transmural perforation associated with Histoplasma capsulatum, confirming gastrointestinal histoplasmosis (Figures 4, 5).

in_text_mentions: Endoscopy revealed multiple ulcers on the base of the tongue and pharynx (as shown in Figure 1). Along with these, there were round to oval organisms surrounded by clear spaces with budding forms within the macrophages, which stained positive for Gomori methenamine silver, suggestive of Histoplasma.

panels.rationale: Single axial contrast-enhanced abdominal CT of a human patient from the article 'Disseminated Histoplasmosis Masquerading as Metastatic Malignancy'. The image visibly shows bilateral heterogeneous suprarenal (adrenal) masses with white arrows and multiple hypodense splenic lesions with red arrows. Bilateral adrenal enlargement with heterogeneous (necrotic) appearance matches the configured vocabulary finding histoplasmosis_bilaterally_enlarged_adrenal_glands, directly attributed to histoplasmosis by the article's disease focus and caption. Splenic hypodensities are additionally recorded as a proposed finding since they are not in the vocabulary. Single-image figure stored whole as panel A with arrows as annotations; no excluded content. [raw subtype: disseminated]
panels.attribution_text: Chanda et al. Disseminated Histoplasmosis Masquerading as Metastatic Malignancy: A Diagnostic Odyssey in an Immunocompromised Host.. Cureus 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.112651. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Axial contrast-enhanced CT images of the abdomen demonstrating (A) a heterogeneous right suprarenal mass (~6.3 × 4.3 × 9.3 cm; white arrow), (B) a heterogeneous left suprarenal mass (~6.8 × 4.2 × 9.8 cm; white arrow), and (C) multiple hypodense lesions involving all poles of the splenic parenchyma (red arrows)
in_text_mentions: The left suprarenal lesion measured 6.8 × 4.2 × 9.8 cm, extending from T11-L1, abutting the tail of the pancreas and the superior pole of the spleen, with maintained fat planes. Multiple well-defined hypodense splenic lesions involving all poles (largest 16 × 13 mm) were also demonstrated (Figure 2).

panels.rationale: Single-panel axial 18F-FDG PET-CT of a human patient with a crosshair-marked left lower lobe pulmonary nodule showing heterogeneous hypermetabolism (SUVmax 7.2, stable 2.4 x 1.8 cm). The disease-focused article title (pulmonary histoplasmosis mimicking recurrent lung adenocarcinoma) together with the captioned manifestation (the left lower lobe nodule that was resected and attributed to histoplasmosis) supports attribution to pulmonary histoplasmosis rather than the mimicked adenocarcinoma. The nodule is mapped to the vocabulary finding calcified pulmonary granuloma (identified visually as the pulmonary nodule/granuloma), and the FDG-avid hypermetabolic nodule is recorded as a proposed finding since it is not in the vocabulary. Presentation is atypical because the granuloma behaved like a hypermetabolic malignancy mimic rather than a quiescent calcified focus. Included as a genuine patient image of the target disease; no third-party restriction, diagram, or other-disease panel is present. [raw subtype: pulmonary]

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: CT chest from a patient with progressive disseminated histoplasmosis (per article title) showing left lung cavitary mass, nodular and ground-glass opacities, and mediastinal lymphadenopathy per caption. Diffuse small nodular opacities visible on the image are consistent with a miliary pattern. Cavitary mass and lymphadenopathy are recognized but less common than classic miliary or calcified presentations in disseminated disease, hence variant typicality. [raw subtype: progressive_disseminated] B: H&E stain from image-guided fine needle aspiration of lung nodules in a patient with progressive disseminated histoplasmosis. Caption states granuloma formation and dimorphic yeast. Granulomatous inflammation with intracellular yeast forms is the classic histopathologic presentation of histoplasmosis. [raw subtype: progressive_disseminated] C: GMS stain from the same lung nodule aspirate showing numerous dimorphic oval-shaped budding yeast...

In the context of disseminated histoplasmosis (article title), these represent CNS involvement. The in-text describes them as 'consistent with pyogenic abscesses secondary to hematogenous infection', introducing some ambiguity, but the article context and prior caption triage support histoplasmosis attribution. Finding not in vocabulary. [raw subtype: disseminated] B: Sagittal contrast CT of thorax showing a retrocardiac rim-enhancing mass (2.7 cm). In the context of disseminated histoplasmosis, this represents mediastinal involvement. The vocabulary finding for calcified fibrosing mediastinal mass requires calcification, which is not mentioned in the caption, so the finding is placed in proposed_findings.
